title: The Courtyard of the Old Exchange (Beurs) in Amsterdam
author: Emanuel de Witte (1617-1692)
license: Public Domain (PD-old-100; artist died 1692) - faithful photographic reproduction of a 2D public domain artwork, Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, Rotterdam
note: Oil on panel, WGA25798. A lower-resolution version of the same painting also exists on Commons (661x690); this is the highest-resolution scan found.

title: Het koffiehuis Quincampoix te Amsterdam, 1720 ("Quinquanpoix") - plate from Het Groote Tafereel der Dwaasheid
author: Anonymous Dutch engraver (satirical print series publisher, 1720)
license: Public Domain (CC0 1.0 Universal - Rijksmuseum Amsterdam public domain dedication)
note: Single bold satirical scene depicting the Quincampoix coffeehouse in Amsterdam (center of local action/wind-trading speculation during the 1720 bubble), from the 74-print album Het Groote Tafereel der Dwaasheid. Rijksmuseum object, decorative border includes reference vignettes to other 1720 bubble schemes.

title: Dojima Rice Exchange, Osaka
author: Yoshimitsu Sasaki (1850-1891)
license: Public Domain (PD-Art / PD-old-100; artist died 1891, life+100)
note: Source: Osaka Prefectural Nakanoshima Library. This is a Meiji-era (not Edo-period) ukiyo-e-style print depicting the historic Dojima Rice Exchange building over the river with its price-signaling flag; no PD Hiroshige/Yoshitora print of Dojima specifically was found on Commons at usable resolution, so this is the closest confirmed-PD match for the venue. Content-accurate for the station (Dojima rice futures market, authorized 1730).

title: The Tontine Coffee House, Wall & Water Streets, about 1797
author: W. M. Aikman (engraver), after a painting by Francis Guy (1760-1820)
license: Public Domain (Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, Popular Graphic Arts collection; pre-1800 print, no known restrictions)
note: CAVEAT: this is the highest-resolution master available from LOC's digitization of this print (confirmed via IIIF info.json, native max = 1024x789) and falls short of the requested 1200px long edge. Wikimedia Commons only hosts small reproductions of the underlying Francis Guy painting (750x485 and smaller) at the New-York Historical Society; no higher-resolution PD scan could be located. Depicts the actual Tontine Coffee House building (left, with flag) at Wall & Water Streets, used by the original 24 brokers shortly after the 1792 Buttonwood Agreement - directly on-topic despite the resolution shortfall.

title: Telegraph ticker receiver / stock ticker for the Gold & Stock Telegraph Company, by Thomas A. Edison
author: Object: Thomas A. Edison (design, 1873 patent no. 140,488); Photo: Jaclyn Nash / Smithsonian NMAH
license: Public Domain / CC0 1.0 (Smithsonian Institution Open Access - work of a Smithsonian employee taken as part of official duties)
note: National Museum of American History object EM*252616. This is a modern (2014) photograph of the genuine historical Edison Gold & Stock Telegraph ticker artifact, not a 19th-century photograph itself, but the depicted object is exactly the Edison stock ticker referenced in the brief and the photo is unambiguously public domain.

title: People gather on the sub-treasury building steps across from the New York Stock Exchange on "Black Thursday"
author: Associated Press
license: Public Domain (published/registered before January 1, 1931, per US copyright law)
note: Iconic, widely-reproduced photo of the crowd outside the NYSE / Federal Hall steps during the October 1929 crash. Three other near-duplicate crowd photos from the same day are also available on Commons at similar resolution if an alternate framing is preferred.

title: Nasdaq MarketSite tower, Times Square, New York
author: ajay_suresh (Flickr)
note: No period (1971) freely-licensed photo of NASDAQ's original all-electronic trading system/terminals was found on Commons - NASDAQ had no physical trading floor at founding, which limits period photography options. This is a modern exterior photo of the Nasdaq MarketSite tower at 4 Times Square, the commercial/public face of NASDAQ since 2000, clearly labelled and unambiguously CC-BY licensed. Web-optimized 900px pair: 1971_nasdaq.webp / 1971_nasdaq_web.jpg.

title: Webvan headquarters, Foster City, California, after the company's bankruptcy
author: Pdanyi (Wikimedia Commons)
license: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International)
note: Webvan was one of the most iconic dot-com bust casualties (online grocery delivery, burned over $1B in venture capital, filed for bankruptcy July 2001). Photo taken the following month shows the quiet, shuttered Foster City HQ with the company sign still visible - a dignified, on-topic, period-authentic representation of the crash without using any copyrighted logo/trademark artwork. Web-optimized 900px pair: 2000_dotcom.webp / 2000_dotcom_web.jpg.

title: Lehman Brothers headquarters, 745 Seventh Avenue, Times Square, New York
author: Arnoldius (Wikimedia Commons)
license: CC BY-SA 3.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported)
note: Rooftop-level view of the Lehman Brothers headquarters building showing the illuminated 'LEHMAN BROTHERS' signage and world-map/clock frieze, taken about 5.5 months before the September 2008 bankruptcy - the same building (now Barclays) referenced in the brief. Dignified building photo, avoids any copyrighted news photography of the collapse itself. Web-optimized 900px pair: 2008_lehman.webp / 2008_lehman_web.jpg.

title: Server room / data center (BalticServers)
author: Fleshas (Wikimedia Commons)
license: CC BY-SA 3.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported)
note: The May 6, 2010 Flash Crash was a purely algorithmic/high-frequency-trading event with no natural photo subject and no NYSE-floor human drama (it happened in electronic order books). This generic, widely-used Commons server-room photo represents the automated trading infrastructure at the root of the event rather than forcing an unrelated trading-floor photo; it is not a photo of the actual systems involved. Web-optimized 900px pair: 2010_flashcrash.webp / 2010_flashcrash_web.jpg.

title: New York Stock Exchange building, empty Broad Street, during the COVID-19 lockdown
author: Anthony Quintano
note: New station (no prior SVG placeholder existed for this one). Shows the NYSE facade with a large American flag and a lone masked pedestrian walking a dog past the deserted, gated building during the March-April 2020 lockdown - a dignified, human-scale image of the market disruption that does not trivialize the public-health crisis. Web-optimized 900px pair: 2020_covid.webp / 2020_covid_web.jpg.

title: GameStop store, Ypsilanti, Michigan
author: Dwight Burdette
note: Neutral storefront photo of a US GameStop retail location (not the specific store involved in the 2021 short squeeze, and not dated to the event itself - no contemporaneous freely-licensed GameStop storefront photo from Jan 2021 was found). Used instead of any Reddit/WallStreetBets screenshot or brokerage-app image, which would raise copyright/ToS concerns. Web-optimized 900px pair: 2021_gamestop.webp / 2021_gamestop_web.jpg.

title: Moscow Exchange (MOEX) main building
author: Fitiss (Wikimedia Commons)
license: CC BY-SA 3.0 (Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported)
note: New station (no prior SVG placeholder existed for this one; a simple oil-barrel/price-chart icon was the suggested fallback if no photo was found). SENSITIVITY: chosen deliberately as a neutral MARKET/ECONOMIC-infrastructure image only - the exterior of the Moscow Exchange building, which halted trading for weeks after the February 2022 invasion. Contains no soldiers, weapons, destruction, refugees, or any combat/conflict imagery whatsoever; only building signage reading 'Московская биржа' (Moscow Exchange). A verified CC BY-SA 3.0 backup candidate also exists (File:Oil_platform_in_the_North_Sea.jpg, Erik Christensen, 2005) representing the oil/gas price-spike angle instead, if this image is ever judged too geopolitically loaded for the context. Web-optimized 900px pair: 2022_ukraine.webp / 2022_ukraine_web.jpg.

title: Bloomberg Terminal and keyboard, dual-monitor trading desk
author: Gforsythe (Wikimedia Commons)
license: Public Domain / CC0 1.0 (Creative Commons Zero, Public Domain Dedication)
note: Clean, unambiguous CC0 photo of a customized dual-monitor Bloomberg Terminal setup with its distinctive color-keyed keyboard - a widely recognizable, generic representation of a modern financial/analyst desk. Web-optimized 900px pair: today_terminal.webp / today_terminal_web.jpg.
